problems.problem: A mushroom is called bad if it contains at least 10 worms. A basket contains 90 bad and 10 good mushrooms. Can all the mushrooms become good after some of the worms crawl from bad mushrooms into good ones?

Rational numbers $a$ and $b$ satisfy the equality
$$a^3b + ab^3 + 2a^2b^2 + 2a + 2b + 1 = 0.$$
Prove that the number $1 - ab$ is the square of a rational number.

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ are drawn. The line perpendicular to the side $AC$ and passing through the point $A_1$ meets the line $B_1C_1$ at a point $D$. Prove that the angle $ADC$ is a right angle.

The figure shows a triangle divided into 25 smaller triangles, numbered from 1 to 25. Can the same numbers be placed in the cells of a $5 \times 5$ square so that any two numbers written in neighbouring triangles are also written in neighbouring cells of the square? (Triangles, like the cells of the square, are considered neighbouring if they share a side.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/rur9_2009_d1_p4_fig.png

Eleven phrases are written on 11 sheets of paper (one on each sheet):
1) There are no sheets with false statements to the left of this sheet.
2) Exactly one sheet to the left of this one contains a false statement.
3) Exactly 2 sheets to the left of this one contain false statements.
$\ldots$
11) Exactly 10 sheets to the left of this one contain false statements.
The sheets were laid out in some order in a row going from left to right. After that some of the written statements became true and some became false. What is the largest possible number of true statements?
A positive integer $m$ is such that the sum of the digits in the decimal representation of the number $8^m$ is equal to 8. Can the last digit of the number $8^m$ be equal to 6?

A parallelogram $ABCD$ with an obtuse angle $ABC$ is given. The line $AD$ meets the circle $\omega$ circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$ for the second time at a point $E$. The line $CD$ meets the circle $\omega$ for the second time at a point $F$. Prove that the circumcentre of the triangle $DEF$ lies on the circle $\omega$.

Eight chess players took part in a chess tournament, and each played every other exactly one game. It is known that any two players who drew their game with each other scored different total numbers of points. Find the largest possible number of draws in this tournament. (A win gives a player 1 point, a draw $\frac{1}{2}$ point, a loss 0.)

Quadratic trinomials $f_1(x) = x^2 + 2a_1x + b_1$, $f_2(x) = x^2 + 2a_2x + b_2$, $f_3(x) = x^2 + 2a_3x + b_3$ are given. It is known that $a_1a_2a_3 = b_1b_2b_3 > 1$. Prove that at least one of these trinomials has two roots.

Seven skiers with numbers $1, 2, \ldots, 7$ left the start one after another and covered the course, each at his own constant speed. It turned out that each skier took part in exactly two overtakings. (Exactly two skiers take part in each overtaking: the one who overtakes and the one who is overtaken.) After the race a record has to be drawn up, consisting of the numbers of the skiers in the order in which they finished. Prove that a race with the described properties can result in at most two different records.

Is it possible, for some positive integer $k$, to split all the positive integers from 1 to $k$ into two groups and write the numbers of each group one after another in some order so that two equal numbers are obtained?

In a triangle $ABC$ the angle $A$ equals $60^\circ$. Let $BB_1$ and $CC_1$ be angle bisectors of this triangle. Prove that the point symmetric to the vertex $A$ with respect to the line $B_1C_1$ lies on the side $BC$.

Neznaika wrote 11 positive integers around a circle. For every two neighbouring numbers he computed their difference. Among the differences found there turned out to be four ones, four twos and three threes. Prove that Neznaika made a mistake somewhere.

Let the points $A$, $B$, $C$ lie on a circle, and let a line $b$ touch this circle at the point $B$. From a point $P$ lying on the line $b$, perpendiculars $PA_1$ and $PC_1$ are dropped to the lines $AB$ and $BC$, respectively (the points $A_1$ and $C_1$ lie on the segments $AB$ and $BC$). Prove that $A_1C_1 \perp AC$.

In a company of seven people, any six can be seated at a round table so that every two neighbours are acquainted. Prove that the whole company can also be seated at a round table so that every two neighbours are acquainted.

For every positive integer $n$ denote by $S_n$ the sum of the first $n$ primes: $S_1 = 2$, $S_2 = 2 + 3 = 5$, $S_3 = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10$, $\ldots$. Can two consecutive terms of the sequence $(S_n)$ both be squares of positive integers?

About three positive numbers it is known that if one chooses one of them and adds to it the sum of the squares of the other two, then the same sum is obtained regardless of the chosen number. Is it true that all the numbers are equal?

An isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($AB = AC$) is given. A point $D$ is taken on the smaller arc $AB$ of its circumcircle. On the extension of the segment $AD$ beyond the point $D$ a point $E$ is chosen so that the points $A$ and $E$ lie in the same half-plane with respect to $BC$. The circumcircle of the triangle $BDE$ meets the side $AB$ at a point $F$. Prove that the lines $EF$ and $BC$ are parallel.

A closed non-self-intersecting broken line is drawn through the centres of some cells of an $8 \times 8$ chessboard. Each segment of the broken line joins the centres of cells that are neighbouring horizontally, vertically or diagonally. Prove that in the polygon bounded by it the total area of the black parts equals the total area of the white parts.

Positive numbers $x$, $y$, $z$ are given. Prove the inequality
$$\frac{x+1}{y+1} + \frac{y+1}{z+1} + \frac{z+1}{x+1} \leqslant \frac{x}{y} + \frac{y}{z} + \frac{z}{x}.$$
Find all numbers $a$ such that for every positive integer $n$ the number $an(n+2)(n+4)$ is an integer.

Initially three distinct points were marked in the plane. Every minute some three of the marked points were chosen, call them $A$, $B$ and $C$, after which the point $D$ symmetric to $A$ with respect to the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ was marked in the plane.

After a day it turned out that among the marked points there were three distinct points lying on a line. Prove that the three initial points also lay on a line.
Find all triples of primes $p$, $q$, $r$ such that the fourth power of any of them, decreased by 1, is divisible by the product of the other two.

A straight stick 2 metres long was sawn into $N$ sticks, the length of each of which is an integer number of centimetres. For what smallest $N$ can one guarantee that, using all the resulting sticks and without breaking them, one can form the outline of some rectangle?

Several numbers are written on the board. It is known that the square of any written number is greater than the product of any two other written numbers. What is the largest possible number of numbers on the board?

Circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ touch externally at a point $P$. A line $\ell_1$ tangent to $\omega_2$ is drawn through the centre of $\omega_1$. Similarly, a line $\ell_2$ touches $\omega_1$ and passes through the centre of $\omega_2$. It turned out that the lines $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ are not parallel. Prove that the point $P$ lies on the bisector of one of the angles formed by $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$.

30 people, knights and liars, sit at a round table (knights always tell the truth and liars always lie). It is known that each of them has exactly one friend, and a knight's friend is a liar while a liar's friend is a knight (friendship is always mutual). To the question "Is your friend sitting next to you?" every other person (sitting in alternate seats) answered "yes". How many of the rest could also have answered "yes"? (List all the possibilities and prove that there are no others.)
Integers $a$ and $b$ are such that for any positive integers $m$ and $n$ the number $am^2 + bn^2$ is a perfect square. Prove that $ab = 0$.

A magician lays out 36 cards in 6 columns of 6 cards and asks a spectator to choose a card mentally and remember the column containing it. After that the magician gathers the cards in a certain way, lays them out again as a $6 \times 6$ square and asks the spectator to name the numbers of the columns containing the chosen card the first and the second time. After the spectator's answer the magician guesses the card without fail. How should the magician act so that the trick is guaranteed to succeed?
Numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that $a^3 - b^3 = 2$ and $a^5 - b^5 \geqslant 4$. Prove that $a^2 + b^2 \geqslant 2$.

An arbitrary point $D$ is marked on the side $AC$ of a triangle $ABC$. Let $E$ and $F$ be the points symmetric to the point $D$ with respect to the bisectors of the angles $A$ and $C$, respectively. Prove that the midpoint of the segment $EF$ lies on the line $A_0C_0$, where $A_0$ and $C_0$ are the points of tangency of the incircle of the triangle $ABC$ with the sides $BC$ and $AB$, respectively.

An $n \times n$ square is given. Initially its cells are coloured white and black in a chessboard pattern, and at least one of the corner cells is black. In one move it is allowed to recolour simultaneously the four cells of some $2 \times 2$ square according to the following rule: each white cell is recoloured black, each black cell green, and each green cell white. For which $n$ can one obtain, after several moves, a chessboard colouring in which black and white have swapped places?

Positive integers $M$ and $N$, both greater than ten, have the same number of digits and satisfy $M = 3N$. To obtain the number $M$, one has to add 2 to one of the digits of $N$ and add an odd digit to each of the remaining digits. What digit could the number $N$ end with? Find all possible answers.

The circle inscribed in a right triangle $ABC$ with hypotenuse $AB$ touches its sides $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ at the points $A_1$, $B_1$, $C_1$, respectively. Let $B_1H$ be an altitude of the triangle $A_1B_1C_1$. Prove that the point $H$ lies on the bisector of the angle $CAB$.

Can a $12 \times 12$ board be divided into L-shaped corners of three neighbouring cells (shown in the figure) so that every horizontal and every vertical row of cells of the board meets the same number of corners? (A row meets a corner if it contains at least one of its cells.)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/rur9_2013_d1_p3_fig.png

1000 numbers are written around a circle. Petya computed the absolute values of the differences of neighbouring numbers, Vasya the absolute values of the differences of numbers one apart (with one number between them), and Tolya the absolute values of the differences of numbers two apart (with two numbers between them). It is known that every one of Petya's numbers is at least twice as large as any of Vasya's numbers. Prove that every one of Tolya's numbers is not less than any of Vasya's numbers.

Nonzero numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that the equation
$$a(x - a)^2 + b(x - b)^2 = 0$$
has a unique solution. Prove that $|a| = |b|$.

Thirty girls, 13 in red dresses and 17 in blue dresses, danced in a ring around a New Year tree. Afterwards each of them was asked whether her neighbour on the right was in a blue dress. It turned out that exactly those girls answered correctly who stood between two girls in dresses of the same colour. How many girls could have answered in the affirmative?

The perpendicular bisector of the side $AC$ of an acute triangle $ABC$ meets the lines $AB$ and $BC$ at the points $B_1$ and $B_2$, respectively, and the perpendicular bisector of the side $AB$ meets the lines $AC$ and $BC$ at the points $C_1$ and $C_2$, respectively. The circles circumscribed about the triangles $BB_1B_2$ and $CC_1C_2$ meet at the points $P$ and $Q$. Prove that the circumcentre of the triangle $ABC$ lies on the line $PQ$.

The numbers $1$ and $-1$ are placed in the cells of an $8 \times 8$ board (one number in each cell). Consider all possible placements on the board of the four-cell T-shaped figure shown in the figure (the figure may be rotated, but its cells must not go outside the board). Call such a placement unsuccessful if the sum of the numbers in the four cells of the figure is not equal to 0. Find the smallest possible number of unsuccessful placements.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/rur9_2013_d2_p4_fig.png

111 distinct positive integers not exceeding 500 are placed around a circle. Could it happen that for each of these numbers its last digit coincides with the last digit of the sum of all the other numbers?
In a quadrilateral $ABCD$ the sides $AD$ and $BC$ are parallel. Prove that if the bisectors of the angles $DAC$, $DBC$, $ACB$ and $ADB$ form a rhombus, then $AB = CD$.

A teacher wrote four distinct positive integers in Petya's notebook. For each pair of these numbers Petya found their greatest common divisor. He obtained six numbers: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ and $N$, where $N > 5$. What is the smallest possible value of $N$?

All cells of a $100 \times 100$ square table are numbered in some order by the numbers from 1 to 10000. Petya paints cells according to the following rules. First he paints $k$ cells of his choice. Then, in each move, Petya may paint one not yet painted cell with number $a$ if at least one of two conditions holds for it: either there is an already painted cell with a number less than $a$ in the same row, or there is an already painted cell with a number greater than $a$ in the same column. For what smallest $k$ can Petya, regardless of the initial numbering, paint all cells of the table in several moves?
A number $x$ is such that exactly one of the four numbers $x - \sqrt{2}$, $x - 1/x$, $x + 1/x$, $x^2 + 2\sqrt{2}$ is not an integer. Find all such $x$.

There are 2013 cards with the digit 1 written on them and 2013 cards with the digit 2. Vasya makes a 4026-digit number out of these cards. In one move Petya may swap some two cards and pay Vasya 1 rouble. The process ends when Petya obtains a number divisible by 11. What is the largest amount Vasya can earn if Petya tries to pay as little as possible?

A cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ is given. The rays $AB$ and $DC$ meet at a point $K$. It turned out that the points $B$, $D$ and the midpoints of the segments $AC$ and $KC$ lie on one circle. What values can the angle $ADC$ take?
Which of the numbers is greater: $(100!)!$ or $99!^{100!} \cdot 100!^{99!}$? (Recall that $n! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot \ldots \cdot n$.)

2015 people sit at a round table, each of them either a knight or a liar. Knights always tell the truth, liars always lie. Each of them was given a card with a number on it, and all the numbers on the cards are distinct. Having looked at the cards of the neighbours, each of the people at the table said: "My number is greater than the number of each of my two neighbours." After that $k$ of those sitting said: "My number is less than the number of each of my two neighbours." For what largest $k$ could this have happened?
Call a positive integer interesting if the sum of its digits is a prime. What is the largest possible number of interesting numbers among five consecutive positive integers?

An equilateral triangle with side 3 is divided into nine triangular cells as shown in the figure. Initially zeros are written in these cells. In one move one may choose two numbers in cells sharing a side and either add one to both or subtract one from both. Petya wants to make several moves so that afterwards the cells contain, in some order, the consecutive positive integers $n, n+1, \ldots, n+8$. For which $n$ can he do this?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/rur9_2015_d1_p3_fig.png

In a scalene triangle $ABC$ the bisectors of the angle $ABC$ and of the angle adjacent to it are drawn. They meet the line $AC$ at the points $B_1$ and $B_2$, respectively. From the points $B_1$ and $B_2$ tangents to the incircle of the triangle $ABC$, different from the line $AC$, are drawn. They touch this circle at the points $K_1$ and $K_2$, respectively. Prove that the points $B$, $K_1$ and $K_2$ are collinear.

After watching a film, viewers rated it one after another with an integer number of points from 0 to 10. At every moment the rating of the film was computed as the sum of all marks given divided by their number. At some moment $T$ the rating turned out to be an integer, and after that it decreased by one with each new voting viewer. What is the largest possible number of viewers who could have voted after the moment $T$?

A right triangle $ABC$ with right angle $C$ is given. Let $BK$ be an angle bisector of this triangle. The circle circumscribed about the triangle $AKB$ meets the side $BC$ for the second time at a point $L$. Prove that $CB + CL = AB$.
Numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are such that $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 = 4$. Prove that $(2 + a)(2 + b) \geqslant cd$.

Petya wants to write out all possible sequences of 100 positive integers in each of which the number 3 occurs at least once, and any two neighbouring terms differ by at most 1. How many sequences will he have to write out?

Quadratic trinomials $f_1(x), f_2(x), \ldots, f_{100}(x)$ are given with equal coefficients of $x^2$, equal coefficients of $x$, but distinct constant terms; each of them has two roots. For each trinomial $f_i(x)$ one root was chosen and denoted by $x_i$. What values can the sum $f_2(x_1) + f_3(x_2) + \ldots + f_{100}(x_{99}) + f_1(x_{100})$ take?

An isosceles triangle $ABC$ with $AB = BC$ is given. In the circle $\Omega$ circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$ the diameter $CC'$ is drawn. The line through the point $C'$ parallel to $BC$ meets the segments $AB$ and $AC$ at the points $M$ and $P$, respectively. Prove that $M$ is the midpoint of the segment $C'P$.

Petya chose several consecutive positive integers and wrote each of them either with a red or with a blue pencil (both colours are present). Can the sum of the least common multiple of all the red numbers and the least common multiple of all the blue numbers be a power of two?

King Hiero has 11 metal ingots that look identical; the king knows that their weights are (in some order) $1, 2, \ldots, 11$ kg. He also has a bag that will tear if more than 11 kg is put into it. Archimedes has found out the weights of all the ingots and wants to prove to Hiero that the first ingot weighs 1 kg. In one step he may load several ingots into the bag and show Hiero that the bag has not torn (tearing the bag is not allowed!). What is the smallest number of loadings of the bag with which Archimedes can achieve his goal?

There are 23 pupils in a class. During the year each pupil of the class celebrated a birthday once, and some (at least one, but not all) of his classmates came to it. Could it happen that every two pupils of this class met at such celebrations the same number of times? (It is assumed that at each party any two guests met, and also the person celebrating met all the guests.)

Call a nonempty (finite or infinite) set $A$ of positive integers complete if for any positive integers $a$ and $b$ (not necessarily distinct and not necessarily lying in $A$) such that $a + b$ lies in $A$, the number $ab$ also lies in $A$. Find all complete sets of positive integers.

Some cells of a white $2016 \times 2016$ table were painted black. Call a positive integer $k$ lucky if $k \leqslant 2016$ and in each of the $k \times k$ grid squares located in the table exactly $k$ cells are painted. (For example, if all cells are black, then only the number 1 is lucky.) What is the largest possible number of lucky numbers?
A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $\angle DAB = 90^\circ$ is given. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$. It turned out that $\angle ADC = \angle BAM$. Prove that $\angle ADB = \angle CAM$.
In a product of three positive integers, each factor was decreased by 3. Could the product have increased by exactly 2016 as a result?

Vasya has chosen 8 cells of a chessboard, no two of which lie in the same row or the same column. In one move Petya places 8 rooks on the board, no two attacking each other, and then Vasya points out all the rooks standing on the chosen cells. If the number of rooks pointed out by Vasya in this move is even (i.e. 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8), then Petya wins; otherwise all the pieces are removed from the board and Petya makes the next move. In what smallest number of moves can Petya guarantee a win?
Does there exist a triangle with sides $x$, $y$ and $z$ such that $x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = (x + y)(y + z)(z + x)$?

An equilateral triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle $\Omega$ and circumscribed about a circle $\omega$. Points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen on the sides $AC$ and $AB$, respectively, so that the segment $PQ$ touches $\omega$. The circle $\Omega_b$ with centre $P$ passes through $B$, and the circle $\Omega_c$ with centre $Q$ passes through $C$. Prove that the circles $\Omega$, $\Omega_b$ and $\Omega_c$ have a common point.

Oleg drew an empty $50 \times 50$ table and wrote a number above each column and to the left of each row. It turned out that all 100 written numbers are distinct, and 50 of them are rational while the remaining 50 are irrational. Then in each cell of the table he wrote the sum of the numbers written next to its row and its column (an "addition table"). What is the largest number of sums in this table that could be rational?

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the median $AM$ and the altitude $BH$ are drawn. The perpendicular to the line $AM$ erected at the point $M$ meets the ray $HB$ at a point $K$. Prove that if $\angle MAC = 30^\circ$, then $AK = BC$.
A convex polygon is cut by non-intersecting diagonals into isosceles triangles. Prove that this polygon has two equal sides.

Initially 100 cards were put on a table, each with a positive integer written on it; exactly 43 of the cards had odd numbers. Then every minute the following procedure was carried out. For every three cards lying on the table, the product of the numbers written on them was computed, all these products were added, and the resulting number was written on a new card, which was added to those lying on the table. A year after the start of the process it turned out that there was a card on the table with a number divisible by $2^{10000}$. Prove that a number divisible by $2^{10000}$ was on one of the cards already one day after the start.
Divide some grid square into grid squares so that not all the small squares are equal, but there is the same number of small squares of each size.
Five positive integers are written on the board. It turned out that the sum of any three of them is divisible by each of the other two. Must there be four equal numbers among them?
A point $E$ is chosen inside a parallelogram $ABCD$ so that $AE = DE$ and $\angle ABE = 90^\circ$. The point $M$ is the midpoint of the segment $BC$. Find the angle $DME$.

A confectionery factory produces $N$ kinds of sweets. For the New Year the factory gave each of the 1000 pupils of a school a present containing sweets of several kinds (the contents of the presents could differ). Every pupil noticed that for any 11 kinds of sweets he had received a sweet of at least one of these kinds. However, it turned out that for any two kinds there is a pupil who received a sweet of exactly one of these two kinds. Find the largest possible value of $N$.

Numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ satisfy the condition $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1$. Prove that
$$(x - y)(y - z)(x - z) \leqslant \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$$
All positive integers with digit sum 2018 are written in increasing order on an infinite paper tape. Which number is written in the 225th place?

Initially 40 blue, 30 red and 20 green counters are placed around a circle, the counters of each colour standing consecutively. In one move one may swap a blue and a red counter standing next to each other, or a blue and a green counter standing next to each other. Can one achieve, after several such operations, that any two neighbouring counters have different colours?

Seryozha chose two distinct primes $p$ and $q$. He considers a positive integer $n$ good if the number $p + q$ can be represented as a sum of exactly $q$ numbers each of which has the form $n^k$ with a nonnegative integer $k$. (For example, if Seryozha had chosen $p = 7$ and $q = 3$, he would consider the number $n = 2$ good, since $7 + 3 = 2^3 + 2^0 + 2^0$.) Prove that Seryozha considers at most two numbers good.

In a circle $\omega$ with centre $O$ non-intersecting chords $AB$ and $CD$ are drawn so that $\angle AOB = \angle COD = 120^\circ$. The tangent to $\omega$ at the point $A$ meets the ray $CD$ at a point $X$, and the tangent to $\omega$ at the point $B$ meets the ray $DC$ at a point $Y$. The line $\ell$ passes through the circumcentres of the triangles $DOX$ and $COY$. Prove that $\ell$ touches $\omega$.

In a company of 100 children, some children are friends (friendship is always mutual). It is known that whichever child is singled out, the remaining 99 children can be divided into 33 groups of three people so that in each group all three are pairwise friends. Find the smallest possible number of pairs of friends.
Two monic quadratic trinomials $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are such that each of them has two roots, and the equalities $f(1) = g(2)$ and $g(1) = f(2)$ hold. Find the sum of all four roots of these trinomials.

Each of 10 people is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a liar, who always lies. Each of them thought of some integer. Then the first said: "My number is greater than 1", the second said: "My number is greater than 2", $\ldots$, the tenth said: "My number is greater than 10". After that all ten, speaking in some order, said: "My number is less than 1", "My number is less than 2", $\ldots$, "My number is less than 10" (each said exactly one of these ten phrases). What is the largest possible number of knights among these 10 people?

100 distinct positive integers are placed around a circle. Vasya divided each of them with remainder by the next one clockwise; it turned out that the remainders obtained by Vasya take only two distinct values. Petya divided each of the numbers with remainder by the next one counterclockwise. Prove that all the remainders obtained by Petya are distinct.

The altitudes of an acute triangle $ABC$ meet at a point $H$. Points $B_1$ and $C_1$ are marked on the segments $BH$ and $CH$, respectively, so that $B_1C_1 \parallel BC$. It turned out that the centre of the circle $\omega$ circumscribed about the triangle $B_1HC_1$ lies on the line $BC$. Prove that the circle $\Gamma$ circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$ touches the circle $\omega$.

Each face of a $1000 \times 1000 \times 1000$ cube is divided into $1000^2$ square cells of side 1. What is the largest number of these cells that can be painted so that no two painted cells share a side?
Four consecutive positive integers greater than 100 are given. Prove that one can choose three of them whose sum can be represented as the product of three distinct positive integers greater than 1.

Several cardboard rectangles lie on a rectangular table. Their sides are parallel to the sides of the table. The sizes of the rectangles may differ and they may overlap, but no two rectangles may have 4 common vertices. Could it happen that every point that is a vertex of a rectangle is a vertex of exactly three rectangles?

A triangle $ABC$ is given. On the external bisector of the angle $ABC$ a point $D$ is marked, lying inside the angle $BAC$, such that $\angle BCD = 60^\circ$. It is known that $CD = 2AB$. The point $M$ is the midpoint of the segment $BD$. Prove that the triangle $AMC$ is isosceles.

A convex $n$-gon ($n \geqslant 4$) is drawn on the board. Each of its vertices has to be painted either black or white. Call a diagonal multicoloured if its endpoints have different colours. Call a colouring of the vertices good if the $n$-gon can be divided into triangles by multicoloured diagonals having no common points (except vertices). Find the number of good colourings.

Petya and Vasya play the following game. Petya chooses 100 (not necessarily distinct) nonnegative numbers $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{100}$ whose sum equals 1. Vasya splits them into 50 pairs as he wishes, computes the product of the numbers in each pair and writes on the board the largest of the 50 products obtained. Petya wants the number on the board to be as large as possible, and Vasya wants it to be as small as possible. What number will be on the board with correct play?

Initially there were 10 piles of sweets on the table, containing $1, 2, \ldots, 10$ sweets, respectively. Malysh decided to redistribute the sweets. Every odd minute he chooses one of the piles and divides it into two piles, each containing at least one sweet. Every even minute he chooses two piles and merges them into one (thus his first action is to divide a pile into two). Can it happen at some moment that all piles on the table contain the same number of sweets?

$n$ distinct integers are written on the board, any two of which differ by at least 10. The sum of the squares of the three largest of them is less than three million. The sum of the squares of the three smallest of them is also less than three million. For what largest $n$ is this possible?

Kolya and Dima play a game on an $8 \times 8$ board, moving alternately; Dima starts. Kolya draws crosses in cells, and Dima covers pairs of side-adjacent cells of the board with $1 \times 2$ rectangles (dominoes). On his move Kolya must put one cross into any empty cell (i.e. a cell in which no cross has been drawn yet and which is not yet covered by a domino). On his move Dima must cover with a domino two adjacent cells (not yet covered by other dominoes) containing an even total number of crosses (0 or 2). The player who cannot make a move loses. Which of the players has a winning strategy?

Let $p$ be a prime greater than 3. Prove that there exists a positive integer $y$ less than $p/2$ such that the number $py + 1$ cannot be represented as a product of two integers each greater than $y$.

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is circumscribed about a circle $\omega$. Prove that the diameter of the circle $\omega$ does not exceed the length of the segment joining the midpoints of the sides $BC$ and $AD$.

Petya and Misha start from the same point on a circular track, running counterclockwise. Both run at constant speeds, Misha's speed being $2\%$ greater than Petya's. Petya always runs counterclockwise, while Misha may change the direction of running at any moment immediately before which he has run half a lap or more in one direction. Show that while Petya runs his first lap, Misha can draw level with him (meet him or catch up with him) three times, not counting the moment of the start.

A green chameleon always tells the truth, while a brown chameleon lies and immediately afterwards turns green. In a company of 2019 chameleons (green and brown), each in turn answered the question of how many of them are green at the moment. The answers were the numbers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2019$ (in some order, not necessarily the one given above). What is the largest possible number of green chameleons at the start?

In an acute triangle $ABC$ the angle bisector $BL$ is drawn. The circle circumscribed about the triangle $ABL$ meets the side $BC$ at a point $D$. It turned out that the point $S$ symmetric to the point $C$ with respect to the line $DL$ lies on the side $AB$ and does not coincide with its endpoints. What values can $\angle ABC$ take?

Call a polygon good if it has a pair of parallel sides. A regular polygon was cut by diagonals not intersecting (at interior points) into several polygons so that all these polygons have the same odd number of sides. Can it happen that at least one of these polygons is good?

Prove that for any positive $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_9$ the inequality
$$\frac{x_1 - x_3}{x_1x_3 + 2x_2x_3 + x_2^2} + \frac{x_2 - x_4}{x_2x_4 + 2x_3x_4 + x_3^2} + \ldots + \frac{x_8 - x_1}{x_8x_1 + 2x_9x_1 + x_9^2} + \frac{x_9 - x_2}{x_9x_2 + 2x_1x_2 + x_1^2} \geqslant 0$$
holds.

Eeyore the donkey made two triangles out of six sticks. Then he took the triangles apart and painted the six sticks in two colours: the three shortest yellow and the other three green. Will the donkey necessarily be able to make two triangles, one of the three yellow sticks and the other of the three green ones?
Two nonzero numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfy the inequalities $x^2 - x > y^2$ and $y^2 - y > x^2$. What sign can the product $xy$ have?

Consider positive integers $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that the fraction
$$k = \frac{ab + c^2}{a + b}$$
is a positive integer less than $a$ and $b$. What is the smallest possible number of positive divisors of the number $a + b$?

Circles $\Omega$ and $\omega$ touch each other internally at a point $A$. In the larger circle $\Omega$ a chord $CD$ is drawn touching $\omega$ at a point $B$ (the chord $AB$ is not a diameter of $\omega$). The point $M$ is the midpoint of the segment $AB$. Prove that the circle circumscribed about the triangle $CMD$ passes through the centre of $\omega$.

Petya and Vasya play on a $100 \times 100$ board. Initially all cells of the board are white. With each of his moves Petya paints black one or several white cells standing consecutively along a diagonal. With each of his moves Vasya paints black one or several white cells standing consecutively along a vertical. (The figure shows possible first moves of Petya and Vasya on a $4 \times 4$ board.) Petya makes the first move. The player who cannot make a move loses. Who wins with correct play?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/rur9_2021_d1_p5_fig.png
Ten-digit positive integers $a$, $b$, $c$ are such that $a + b = c$. What is the largest possible number of odd digits among their 30 digits?

Vasya wrote the positive integers from 1 to 81 in the cells of a $9 \times 9$ table (one number in each cell, all numbers distinct). It turned out that any two numbers differing by 3 stand in cells sharing a side. Is it true that there must be two corner cells the difference of whose numbers is divisible by 6?

A trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AD$ and $BC$ is given. It turned out that the centroid (the intersection point of the medians) of the triangle $ABD$ lies on the bisector of the angle $BCD$. Prove that the centroid of the triangle $ABC$ lies on the bisector of the angle $ADC$.

An alphabet has $n > 1$ letters; a word is any finite sequence of letters in which any two neighbouring letters are distinct. A word is called good if it is impossible to delete all its letters except four so that what remains is a sequence of the form $aabb$, where $a$ and $b$ are distinct letters. Find the largest possible number of letters in a good word.

Vitya wrote $n$ distinct positive integers in a notebook. For each pair of numbers from the notebook he wrote their least common multiple on the board. Could it happen, for some $n > 100$, that the $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ numbers on the board are (in some order) consecutive terms of a non-constant arithmetic progression?

One day after classes Misha wrote ten positive integers on a sheet of paper. All ten numbers are pairwise distinct. It is known that three numbers divisible by 5 can be chosen from the ten written numbers. It is also known that four numbers divisible by 4 can be chosen from the ten written numbers. Can the sum of all the written numbers be less than 75?

A positive integer $N$ was written nine times on the board (one under another). Petya appended to each of the 9 numbers, on the left or on the right, one nonzero digit; all the appended digits are distinct. What is the largest possible number of primes among the 9 resulting numbers?

A quadratic trinomial $P(x)$, not necessarily with integer coefficients, is given. It is known that for some integers $a$ and $b$ the difference $P(a) - P(b)$ is the square of a positive integer. Prove that there exist more than a million pairs of integers $(c, d)$ such that the difference $P(c) - P(d)$ is also the square of a positive integer.

In a company some pairs of people are friends (if $A$ is friends with $B$, then $B$ is friends with $A$). It turned out that among every 100 people of the company the number of pairs of friends is odd. Find the largest possible number of people in such a company.

Let $CE$ be an angle bisector of an acute triangle $ABC$. A point $D$ is marked on the external bisector of the angle $ACB$, and a point $F$ on the side $BC$, so that $\angle BAD = 90^\circ = \angle DEF$. Prove that the circumcentre of the triangle $CEF$ lies on the line $BD$.

A sequence of numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2022}$ is such that $a_n - a_k \geqslant n^3 - k^3$ for all $n$ and $k$ with $1 \leqslant n \leqslant 2022$ and $1 \leqslant k \leqslant 2022$. Moreover, $a_{1011} = 0$. What values can $a_{2022}$ take?

Petya divided a $100 \times 100$ grid square in some way into dominoes, i.e. $1 \times 2$ grid rectangles, and in each domino joined the centres of its two cells by a blue segment. Vasya wants to divide the same square into dominoes in a second way and in each of his dominoes join the two cells by a red segment. Vasya wants to achieve that from every cell one can reach any other cell moving along the blue and red segments. Will he necessarily be able to do this?

In a trapezoid $ABCD$ the diagonal $BD$ is equal to the base $AD$. The diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ meet at a point $E$. A point $F$ on the segment $AD$ is chosen so that $EF \parallel CD$. Prove that $BE = DF$.
$N$ points are marked in the plane. Any three of them form a triangle whose angles, measured in degrees, are positive integers. For what largest $N$ is this possible?
Prove that there exists a positive integer $b$ such that for every positive integer $n > b$ the sum of the digits of the number $n!$ is at least $10^{100}$.

A cycle track consists of two sections: first an asphalt one, then a sandy one. Petya and Vasya started separately (first Petya, then Vasya), and each rode the whole track. The speed of each boy on each of the two sections was constant. It turned out that they drew level in the middle of the asphalt section and also in the middle of the sandy one. Which of the boys spent less time on the whole track?

A paper triangle with side lengths 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm is given. Can it be cut into several (more than one) polygons each of which has area (measured in cm$^2$) numerically equal to its perimeter (measured in cm)?

A positive integer $n$ is given. $2n$ rooks were placed on a $2n \times 2n$ board so that no two of them stand in the same row or the same column. After that the board was cut along the grid lines into two connected parts symmetric to each other with respect to the centre of the board. What is the largest possible number of rooks in one of the parts? (A grid figure is called connected if from any of its cells one can reach any other cell within the figure, moving each time to a cell sharing a side.)
Positive integers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are given. None of them is a multiple of another. It is known that the number $abc + 1$ is divisible by $ab - b + 1$. Prove that $c \geqslant b$.

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle $\gamma$. It turned out that the circles constructed on the segments $AB$ and $CD$ as diameters touch each other externally at a point $S$. Let the points $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the segments $AB$ and $CD$, respectively. Prove that the perpendicular $\ell$ to the line $MN$ erected at the point $M$ meets the line $CS$ at a point lying on $\gamma$.
For a positive integer $n$ denote by $S_n$ the least common multiple of all the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, n$. Does there exist a positive integer $m$ such that $S_{m+1} = 4S_m$?

99 numbers, no two of them equal, were written on the board. In a notebook $\frac{99 \cdot 98}{2}$ numbers were written down: all the differences of two numbers from the board (each time the smaller number was subtracted from the larger one). It turned out that the number 1 was written in the notebook exactly 85 times. Let $d$ be the largest number written in the notebook. Find the smallest possible value of $d$.

An acute triangle $ABC$ with $AB < BC$ is given. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the sides $AB$ and $AC$, respectively, and let $H$ be the foot of the altitude dropped from the vertex $B$. The incircle touches the side $AC$ at a point $K$. The line through $K$ parallel to $MH$ meets the segment $MN$ at a point $P$. Prove that a circle can be inscribed in the quadrilateral $AMPK$.

Find the largest number $m$ such that for any positive numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ whose sum equals 1 the inequality
$$\sqrt{\frac{ab}{c + ab}} + \sqrt{\frac{bc}{a + bc}} + \sqrt{\frac{ca}{b + ca}} \geqslant m$$
holds.

A $100 \times 100 \times 100$ cube is divided into a million unit cubes; there is a light bulb in each small cube. Three faces of the large cube having a common vertex are painted: one red, another blue and the third green. Call a column a set of 100 small cubes forming a $1 \times 1 \times 100$ block. Each of the 30 000 columns has one painted end cell; in this cell there is a switch, and pressing this switch changes the state of all 100 bulbs of the column (a bulb that is off is switched on, and one that is on is switched off). Initially all bulbs were off. Petya pressed several switches, obtaining a situation in which exactly $k$ bulbs are on. Prove that after that Vasya can press several switches so that no bulb is on, using at most $k/100$ switches on the red face.

Oleg has a set of 2024 distinct grid rectangles of sizes $1 \times 1$, $1 \times 2$, $1 \times 3$, $\ldots$, $1 \times 2024$ (one rectangle of each size). Can he, choosing some of them, assemble a grid square of area greater than 1?

The parabola $y = x^2$ is drawn in the coordinate plane. For a given number $k > 0$ consider the trapezoids inscribed in this parabola (that is, all vertices of the trapezoid lie on the parabola) whose bases are parallel to the $x$-axis and the product of the lengths of whose bases equals $k$. Prove that the diagonals of all such trapezoids pass through one point.

An island is inhabited by knights, who always tell the truth, and liars, who always lie. For a game of "winner stays on" table tennis all inhabitants of the island were divided into two teams $A$ and $B$, team $A$ having more inhabitants than $B$. The game was started by two players from different teams; after each game the loser left the game for good and was replaced by another (not yet played) member of his team. The team all of whose members had left the game lost. After the tournament each member of team $A$ was asked: "Is it true that in some game you lost to a liar?", and each member of team $B$ was asked: "Is it true that you beat at least two knights?". All the answers were affirmative. Which team won, $A$ or $B$?

All positive integers from 1 to 1000 are written in a row in some order, each exactly once. Prove that one can choose several consecutive numbers of the row whose sum is greater than 100000 but does not exceed 100500.

An isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($AB = BC$) is given. On the extensions of the lateral sides $AB$ and $BC$ beyond the point $B$ the points $D$ and $E$, respectively, are marked, and on the base $AC$ a point $F$ is marked, so that $AC = DE$ and $\angle CFE = \angle DEF$. Prove that $\angle ABC = 2\angle DFE$.

7 distinct numbers whose sum equals 10 are written on the board. Petya multiplied each of them by the sum of the other six and wrote the 7 products obtained in his notebook. It turned out that only four distinct numbers occur in the notebook. Find one of the numbers written on the board.

A point is marked on a circle of length 1 metre. Two cockroaches started running from it simultaneously in the same direction with different constant speeds. Every time the fast cockroach caught up with the slow one, the slow one instantly turned around without changing its speed. Every time they met face to face, the fast one instantly turned around without changing its speed. At what distance from the marked point could their hundredth meeting take place?

Points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen on the side $BC$ of an acute triangle $ABC$ so that $BP = PQ = QC$. Points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen on the segments $AC$ and $AB$, respectively, so that $PX \perp AC$ and $QY \perp AB$. Prove that the centroid of the triangle $ABC$ is equidistant from the lines $XQ$ and $YP$.

An equilateral triangle $T$ with side 111 is divided by lines parallel to its sides into equilateral triangles with side 1. All vertices of these triangles except the centre of the triangle $T$ are marked. Call a set of several marked points linear if all these points lie on one line parallel to a side of $T$. In how many ways can all the marked points be partitioned into 111 linear sets? (Ways differing only in the order of the sets are considered the same.)

Does there exist a positive integer $n > 10^{100}$ such that the decimal representations of the numbers $n^2$ and $(n+1)^2$ differ by a permutation of digits? (In other words, the decimal representations of $n^2$ and $(n+1)^2$ must contain equally many digits 0, equally many digits 1, $\ldots$, equally many digits 9.)

A school and the houses of Anya and Borya stand on a straight road. Every day Anya leaves her house at 8:00 and walks to school. One day Borya ran out of his house towards the school at 8:00 and caught up with Anya in 30 minutes. The next day he ran out at 8:10 and caught up with Anya in 40 minutes. At what time should he run out in order to meet Anya as she leaves her house? (Anya's speed is always constant, and so is Borya's.)

In an isosceles triangle $ABC$ ($AB = BC$) the angle bisector $CD$ is drawn. A point $F$ is marked on the base $AC$ so that $BD = CF$. A point $E$ is chosen so that the quadrilateral $CDEF$ is a parallelogram. Prove that $BE = BF$.

Quadratic trinomials $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are given; denote $p_n = P(n)$ and $q_n = Q(n)$. Once a minute Sasha draws a line in the coordinate plane: in the first minute the line with equation $y = p_1x + q_1$, in the second the line $y = p_2x + q_2$, $\ldots$, in the $i$-th minute the line $y = p_ix + q_i$. After some time Sasha found three drawn lines passing through one point. Prove that all drawn lines pass through one point.

A one-rouble coin lies in each cell of a $2 \times 200$ board. Dasha and Sonya play a game, moving alternately; Dasha starts. In one move one may choose any coin and move it: Dasha moves a coin to a diagonally adjacent cell, Sonya to a cell adjacent by a side. If two coins end up in the same cell, one of them is immediately removed from the board and goes to Sonya. Sonya may stop the game at any moment and take all the money she has received. What is the largest amount she can win, however Dasha plays?

Find all pairs of integers $m$ and $n > 2$ such that $((n-1)! - n) \cdot (n-2)! = m(m-2)$.

Recall that $k! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot \ldots \cdot k$ is the product of all positive integers from 1 to $k$.

Sasha took a piece of thread. He folded it in half, then in half again, and so on 10 times. Then he took scissors and cut the resulting construction at one place (thus he cut the thread at 1024 places). As a result the thread fell into pieces. It turned out that the lengths of these pieces take only two distinct values, the smaller of which equals 10 cm. Find all possible values of the length of the original thread.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/rur9_2025_d2_p1_fig.png

Suppose several integers are written on the board (some of which may be equal). Say that these numbers form a lucky set if they cannot be divided into two nonempty groups so that the product of the sum of the numbers in one group and the sum of the numbers in the other group is positive. A teacher wrote several integers on the board. Prove that the children can add exactly one more integer to them so that the resulting set is lucky.

100 two-rouble coins and $N$ five-rouble coins were laid out on a table around a circle in some order. It is known that by choosing several consecutive coins of the circle it is impossible to obtain a sum of exactly 52 roubles. Find the largest possible value of $N$.

12 vessels stand on a table, arranged in 4 rows of 3 vessels each. Some (possibly zero) amount of water is poured into each vessel. It is known that the total amount of water in each row equals 1 litre. For which $\alpha$ can one assert that there are two vessels on the table whose amounts of water differ by at most $\alpha$ litres?

Let $M$ be the midpoint of the side $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$. On the extension of the side $AB$ beyond the point $B$ there is a point $D$ such that $\angle ADM = \angle ACM = 30^\circ$. The point $O$ is the circumcentre of the triangle $ACD$. Find the angle $OBC$.
Numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are such that $a^2 + b^2 < (a - b)^2$ and $b^2 + c^2 < (b - c)^2$. Prove that $a^4 + c^4 < (a + c)^4$.

All 144 vertices of the cells of an $11 \times 11$ grid square were marked. Then the marked points were coloured in five colours. For what largest $d$ could it happen that the distance between any two marked points of the same colour is at least $d$?

Petya and Vasya play a game. At the start of the game there are 1000 piles on the table consisting of $1, 2, 3, 4, \ldots, 999, 1000$ matches, respectively. The boys move alternately; Petya starts. On his move each of the boys may take any nonzero number of matches from a pile with the largest number of matches (from exactly one such pile if there are several). The one who takes the last match wins. Which of the boys can play so as to be guaranteed to win?
Does there exist a positive integer $n$ such that for some three of its divisors $a$, $b$, $c$, greater than 1, the product $(a - 1)(b - 1)(c - 1)$ is divisible by $n^2$?

Convex quadrilaterals $ABCD$ and $KLMN$ are placed so that the lines $KL$, $LM$, $MN$ and $NK$ are the bisectors of the external angles $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ of the quadrilateral $ABCD$, respectively. Moreover, $ABCD$ is not a parallelogram. The diagonals of the quadrilateral $KLMN$ meet at a point $P$. Prove that if $\angle BAD = \angle BCD < 90^\circ$, then $PA = PC$.

A coach gave beginner chess players a task: each of them must come to an $8 \times 8$ chessboard, put a chess king on one of the corner cells and make 21 moves with it so that the king visits some two other corner cells and returns to the initial cell. After that the king is removed and the next child comes to the board. Four children in turn completed the task. Must there then be two cells $A$ and $B$ such that at least two children moved the king from the cell $A$ to the cell $B$?
An odd prime $p$ is given. Find all pairs of positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that $\frac{a}{p} + \frac{p}{b} = 2$.

An acute triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle with centre $O$. The line $AO$ meets the segment $BC$ at a point $D$. A point $E$ is chosen on the segment $BC$ so that $D$ is the midpoint of the segment $CE$. The foot $T$ of the perpendicular dropped from $E$ to $CO$ lies inside the triangle $ABD$. The line $BT$ meets the circle circumscribed about the triangle $ABD$ at a point $K$. Prove that the lines $AK$ and $CO$ are parallel.

Numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are greater than one and satisfy the equality $\left(a - \frac{1}{b}\right)\left(b - \frac{1}{c}\right)\left(c - \frac{1}{a}\right) = 1$. Prove that
$$\left(a - \frac{1}{a}\right)^2 + \left(b - \frac{1}{b}\right)^2 + \left(c - \frac{1}{c}\right)^2 \geqslant \frac{b}{a} + \frac{c}{b} + \frac{a}{c}.$$

In a large company every person has exactly 100 acquaintances in this company (if $A$ is acquainted with $B$, then $B$ is acquainted with $A$). It turned out that among the 100 acquaintances of any person there is at least one pair of people not acquainted with each other. For what largest $k$ can one assert that there is a person in the company among whose 100 acquaintances there are at least $k$ distinct pairs of people, in each of which the people are not acquainted with each other? (One person may belong to several such pairs.)
